rv.q: I was sufficiently impressed by “The October Storm” to wish I had.
All of the elements add up to a wonderful play.
A rich and nuanced exploration of identity, longing, trauma, and hope, The October Storm is as refreshing as the rain.
Allen has written a beautiful slow burn of a play.
Joshua Allen’s second play in his Grand Boulevard Trilogy, each of which is set in a three-flat in Chicago’s Southside, is entertaining and moving.
It's the powerhouse cast and deeply authentic storytelling that make The October Storm a story that does not disappoint.
In “The October Storm,” we are shown that an embrace of growth is synonymous with experiencing fear, and that we must take that leap even though it terrifies us.

It is at the close of the performance (and especially once it is over—and on reflection) that one can fully appreciate the depth of detail and caring that went into the script and how well each of the characters is personified.

cn.t: Critics praise Joshua Allen's richly human South Side drama for expert writing and powerhouse performances, particularly Shariba Rivers. The second installment of his Grand Boulevard Trilogy offers an authentic, warm slice of 1960s Black life.
